name: Umar Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Umar, 43, and I drive a dozer at the large mine, shaping the haul-road edges and clearing loose material after a shift. I have a vocational certificate and know the pit well enough, though I'm an ordinary mid-level operator on the lower pay band. My partner runs a small laundry pickup service, and we have two school-age children, a mortgage and under a month of expenses saved. I use an AI assistant every day to turn maintenance notes into questions and compare maps, but I always check its answers with the survey team before moving earth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew small AI helpers can make fault notes easier to read. The dozer still needs a driver who knows the road edge after rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dozer hours look steady, but our household margin is very small. A slow week in my partner's laundry service can leave the mortgage waiting for overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep shaping the haul road and checking soft edges before each pass. I'd use AI to sort my maintenance notes, then confirm each fault against the machine book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the bills even in the mild picture. My partner's laundry van needed tyres last month, and that used nearly all the emergency money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with an extra shift payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put it straight back in the emergency account after the van tyres. The children both have school trips due this term, and I'd rather have the fee ready than borrow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where can the AI assistant mislead you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once mixed up two warning codes on a dozer I hadn't driven before. The machine book showed the difference. The assistant gives me a question, not an answer I trust alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say survey and dispatch will change faster than the dozer seat. The mine should test new road maps with drivers before setting targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical blade work remains, but AI plans could push us onto unsafe edges. If the mine reduces survey jobs, I could lose the local judgement I ask for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd trial the AI road map with a surveyor on one daytime shift. I'd take photos of soft shoulders before accepting a new route target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the household budget and about a plan that looks tidy on a screen but wrong in the pit. I would try the tool early if the surveyor walks the ground with me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After heavy rain, the south shoulder sinks under the dozer's weight. I'd mark that on the map and stop work there until the surveyor checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the survey team shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the superintendent who signs off the ground checks now. The software may draw the route, but someone must be accountable when a shoulder gives way.

S1.quote: The software may draw the route, but someone must be accountable when a shoulder gives way.
fieldNote: He is quick to **trial a map**, yet insists that the surveyor walk soft ground before a dozer follows it.
**Thinking AI** reaches his job through survey staffing and road targets rather than immediate physical replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew 2028 AGI might replace survey planning first. By 2031, robot dozers could clear the road, so we need named training places now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, I might still drive while AI writes the earthwork plan. At 48 in 2031, the mine could replace my dozer and there are few other mine seats nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enroll in an evening industrial refrigeration course next term while working mine shifts. I'd apply to local cold-store maintenance jobs in the first robot year if dozer work falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because the mortgage and children are still there in 2031, and our savings might cover only weeks. I can move early, but I can't promise a refrigeration job will be safe from robots either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why refrigeration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner picks up uniforms from the local food warehouse, and I helped its technician find a bad door seal last winter. The local food warehouse hires technicians, so I want to ask what certificate it actually needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you afford the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the mine's education allowance covers the first module and keep my full shifts. If it doesn't, I'd start with the free college evening class rather than use the mortgage money.

feel: **Anxious** about possible 2031 dozer cuts, with an early plan.

fieldNote: He sees **2031 robot dozers** as a direct threat and starts preparing while the household still relies on mine pay.
His **refrigeration idea** has a local warehouse lead, but he recognises the new field could also automate.

steps.text: Enroll in funded industrial refrigeration module or free evening class next term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a 2034 fleet timetable before management orders robot dozers. Workers need paid course hours that match real warehouse vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, AGI may do maps and records while I still shape roads. At 51 in 2034, the children will be older, but the mortgage and other bills remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd complete the first refrigeration module next year while I keep driving. I'd put half my weekend premiums into the emergency account until it covers one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about our money now, but five years gives me more room to train without quitting. I can ask warehouse technicians what the work pays before I decide to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move into a mine control room instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn how it works, but I wouldn't treat a screen job as a permanent shelter. AGI could manage maps and controls too, and the warehouse job might offer a wider range of employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your partner help decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd compare both incomes across a school term, because the laundry business gets busy and quiet in stretches. A new wage must cover the mortgage even in its slow month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2039 leaves time to build another skill if the mine shares honest dates. The company should publish fleet numbers by year so people can decide when to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, AI could produce road plans while I still operate the dozer. At 56 in 2039, I may need a new paid job rather than a retirement story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my dozer wage and take one refrigeration unit next year. I'd visit the food warehouse each spring hiring season to check openings and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about current bills, though the long runway takes some pressure off the career decision. I could try a new qualification without betting the house on it immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy machinery for your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the laundry van taught me a lesson. The laundry van already showed how expensive equipment can be. I'd keep spare cash for the mortgage and a course, then decide when I see an actual offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the warehouse manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what a new technician earns and whether there are paid trainee shifts. If the pay falls below the house payment, I'd keep searching while the mine still employs me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robot dozers in 2031 could take the mine wage before we rebuild savings, while both children still need us. A funded course, a clear fleet timetable and a warehouse job that covers the mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the first pay cheque after a move. Even a good training route could leave a month's gap, so I'd want to know when wages actually start.

headlineQuote: Even a good training route could leave a month's gap, so I'd want to know when wages actually start.
portrait: Umar is a **43-year-old** experienced dozer operator with a vocational certificate and lower mine pay.
His partner's laundry business varies, while two school-age children, a **mortgage** and less than a month saved limit risk.
He uses **AI daily** for notes and maps, but checks them against the machine book and survey team.
He pursues **refrigeration training** early and compares local warehouse pay before risking the household wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 robot dozers could end his mine wage while the children still depend on it.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded course**, clear fleet timetable and local job that covers the mortgage would help him move safely.
